network.overall_strategy: The network includes both mechanistically-resolved and detection-based prebiotic routes to proline, using the only demonstrated stepwise route (Patel et al., 2015, Nature Chem.) as the backbone. Ten distinct pathways cover: (1) cyanosulfidic surface photoredox, (2) arginine/ornithine branch cyclization, (3) spark discharge Strecker, (4) interstellar ice photolysis, (5) parent-body alteration in meteorites/asteroids, (6) nebular FTT catalysis, (7) surface Strecker via 4-aminobutanal, (8) hypothetical protometabolic glutamate/P5C reduction, (9) phase-behavior chiral amplification, and (10) chirality transfer from sugars or CPL. Atom and charge balance is strictly maintained for all discrete steps; detection-based and hydrolysis routes are explicitly annotated. Each step is justified and citations provided, with all speculative branches declared. Feedstock selection, intermediate assignment, and reaction families are chosen according to experimental evidence and mechanistic constraint.

reactions.name: Copper(I)-catalyzed coupling of HCN and acetylene to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: mildly alkaline; prebiotic UV; intermittent delivery

reactions.mechanism: Cu(I) mediates nucleophilic attack of HCN on acetylene, forming acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Stepwise, experimentally demonstrated as required for prebiotic proline backbone formation; yields acrylonitrile for both proline and arginine branches (Patel et al., 2015, Nat. Chem.).

reactions.name: Aza-Michael addition of ammonia to acrylonitrile (β-aminopropionitrile formation)

conditions.other: neutral or mildly alkaline; aqueous conditions; no catalyst needed

reactions.mechanism: Direct nucleophilic addition of ammonia to the conjugated double bond of acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This step is mechanistically robust and required for both proline and arginine amino nitrile branches. No catalyst needed (Patel et al. 2015, Nat. Chem.).

reactions.name: Photoreduction of β-aminopropionitrile to β-aminopropanal and on to γ-butyrothiolactam (cyclic thioamide)
reactions.mechanism: UV/HS⁻ partial reduction of the nitrile to an imine/aldehyde, HCN addition (cyanohydrin), then H2S-induced formation of the α-hydroxythioamide. Cyclization and photoreduction yield γ-butyrothiolactam.
reactions.reasoning: All intermediates characterized by Patel et al. (2015, Nat. Chem.); unique to cyanosulfidic chemistry for proline/arginine skeletons and robust against hydrolysis critiques (Ranjan et al. 2018, Astrobiology).

reactions.name: Photoreductive cyclization and Strecker-type cyanation to pyrrolidine-2-carbonitrile (proline α-aminonitrile)
reactions.mechanism: UV/HS− photoreduction of thiolactam to cyclic imine, followed by nucleophilic attack of HCN to yield pyrrolidine-2-carbonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Yield of 32% for these last two steps validated by Patel et al. (2015); cyanation is documented (Sutherland group).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of proline α-aminonitrile to prolinamide, then to L-Proline (final hydrolytic step)
reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nucleophilic water addition: hydrolysis of the nitrile to amide, then further to the acid, with HCN elimination.
reactions.reasoning: Standard hydrolysis; slow but robust under near-neutral or mildly acidic conditions (Patel et al. 2015; supported by general aminonitrile reactivity literature).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of prolinamide to L-Proline
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of amide to carboxylic acid with ammonia loss; proceeds on mineral surfaces.
reactions.reasoning: Standard chemical hydrolysis. While explicit proline yields unreported in Sutherland’s experiments, amide → amino acid hydrolysis is universally established (general principles; speculative for proline step due to lack of direct evidence).

reactions.name: Cyanamide competition – guanidinylation and branching to arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: high cyanamide flux restricts proline flux

reactions.mechanism: Cyanamide intercepts β-aminopropionitrile; forms C–N bond to give arginine skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Competitive branching supported by Patel et al. 2015, with competition at this node explicitly controlling proline vs. arginine outcome.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of arginine aminonitrile to arginine
reactions.mechanism: Aqueous hydrolysis of aminonitrile to carboxylic acid (arginine) plus ammonia loss.
reactions.reasoning: Standard aminonitrile→amino acid hydrolysis. Mechanistic logic is robust, but proline is not produced from this branch (Patel et al. 2015).

reactions.name: Ornithine from arginine by hydrolysis/deglycation (biochemical analogy)
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic removal of the guanidine group from arginine (urea byproduct), yielding ornithine.
reactions.reasoning: Prebiotic ornithine formation via arginine hydrolysis is suggested in metabolic analogy and partially supported in hydrothermal experiments on amino acid degradation (Vallentyne 1968, Körner et al. 2021).

reactions.name: Cyclization of ornithine to proline (hydrothermal deamination)
reactions.mechanism: Nonenzymatic cyclodeamination: α-amino nitrogen attacks δ-carbon, forming proline and liberating NH3.
reactions.reasoning: Reported as a product of arginine/ornithine pyrolysis in Vallentyne (1968) and discussed by Körner et al. (2021); product assignment uncertain (speculative).

reactions.name: Reductive amination of α-ketoglutarate to glutamate (Fe-based hydrothermal catalysis)
agents: Fe0, FeS, Ni0 or meteorite minerals
reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination with H2 and ammonia; converts α-ketoglutarate to glutamic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Experimental demonstration of nonenzymatic glutamate formation in Kitadai et al. 2019; Kaur et al. 2024; no direct prebiotic route to proline, but forms biosynthetic precursor.

reactions.name: Hypothetical reduction of glutamate to 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid (P5C)
reactions.mechanism: Putative, uphill reduction of the γ-carboxyl (or phosphoryl) of glutamic acid to the corresponding aldehyde, which cyclizes to P5C.
reactions.reasoning: No prebiotic demonstration; step is thermodynamically uphill and unproven—annotated as speculative (see literature review, Section 5, and Fichman et al. 2015).

reactions.name: Spontaneous cyclization of GSA to P5C
reactions.mechanism: GSA spontaneously cyclizes nonenzymatically to the cyclic imine P5C.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by reports from Smith & Greenberg (1956). No prebiotic reduction for next step is known.

reactions.name: Speculative reduction of P5C to proline (not experimentally demonstrated)
reactions.mechanism: Reduction of the cyclic imine to secondary amine (proline).
reactions.reasoning: No prebiotic reduction for P5C to proline is published; this is labeled speculative (see literature and Fichman et al. 2015).

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis via 4-aminobutanal (spark discharge scenario, detection route)
reactions.mechanism: Assembly and Strecker cyanation of 4-aminobutanal yields cyclic α-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: No intermediates isolated, detection of proline after hydrolysis is established (Ring et al. 1972; Miller & Urey lineage; Johnson et al. 2008; detection, not stepwise confirmation).

reactions.name: Aqueous/acid hydrolysis of interstellar residues/macro-organics to proline
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of macromolecular or precursor residues yields detectable proline.
reactions.reasoning: Modeled directly on detection of proline in interstellar ice analog photolysis and meteorite hydrolyzates (Muñoz Caro et al. 2002; Glavin et al. 2025; Bernstein et al. 2002). No intermediate/mechanism specified.

reactions.name: Fischer-Tropsch-type nebular catalysis (detection route)

conditions.other: FTT conditions only; mechanism uncharacterized for proline

reactions.mechanism: Unspecified network of CHON polymerization reactions under nebular/planetesimal catalysis generates proline among amino acid mixture.
reactions.reasoning: Amino acids detected after FTT catalysis in meteorites, but no proline mechanism characterized (Hayatsu et al. 1971; Pizzarello 2012).

reactions.name: Spontaneous chiral amplification by solution–solid phase behavior (eutectic enrichment)
reactions.mechanism: Partial enantiomeric excess (ee) in solution at equilibrium with precipitated racemate drives solution toward homochirality.
reactions.reasoning: Extensively characterized for proline in Klussmann et al. 2006. Not prebiotically demonstrated for L-proline but thermodynamically robust; requires seed ee.

reactions.name: Chirality transfer/amplification by CPL or sugars (seed asymmetry)
reactions.mechanism: Enantioselective photolysis by CPL or secondary induction by chiral sugars modestly enriches L-proline.
reactions.reasoning: Documented in extraterrestrial amino acids (de Marcellus et al. 2011) and in laboratory models (Wagner et al. 2017); proline amplification via CPL predicted but not measured.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic photoredox proline synthesis (Patel et al. 2015)
pathways.description: Stepwise cyanosulfidic chemistry from HCN and acetylene through acrylonitrile, aza-Michael addition, UV/HS⁻ photoreduction to β-aminopropionitrile, γ-butyrothiolactam, and Strecker cyanation, hydrolyzed to proline.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic arginine branch (competing, cyanamide-diverted, no proline output)
pathways.description: Acrylonitrile intercepted by cyanamide via β-aminopropionitrile to arginine aminonitrile and finally arginine.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal ornithine/arginine cyclization to proline
pathways.description: Hydrothermal deamination of ornithine (from arginine hydrolytic deguanidinylation) cyclizes to racemic proline.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal protometabolic (glutamate to proline) pathway (speculative)
pathways.description: From α-ketoglutarate, reductive amination forms glutamate, followed by hypothetical reduction to GSA/P5C and cyclization/reduction to proline.

pathways.name: Spark discharge Strecker synthesis via 4-aminobutanal
pathways.description: Formation of 4-aminobutanal by spark discharge or reduction, Strecker cyanation and cyclization to the proline α-aminonitrile and hydrolysis to proline.

pathways.name: Interstellar or meteorite delivery with hydrolytic release (detection only)
pathways.description: Formation of macro-organic residues or precursors in space, with proline released only upon acid hydrolysis on arrival.

pathways.name: Asteroidal/meteoritic parent body alteration (detection only, hydrolysis)
pathways.description: Hydrothermal aqueous alteration on parent bodies generates proline (detection only, no mechanism).

pathways.name: Nebular Fischer-Tropsch-type catalysis (detection only)
pathways.description: CO, NH3, and H2 (from the solar nebula) are catalytically converted to a suite of amino acids, including proline, by meteoritic metals.

pathways.name: Chiral amplification by phase behavior (eutectic enrichment)
pathways.description: Proline formed racemically by any route undergoes chiral amplification by precipitation/solution equilibrium, resulting in L-proline enrichment.

pathways.name: Chirality transfer by CPL or chiral sugars
pathways.description: Small initial L-excess in proline, derived from CPL-irradiated precursors or chiral sugars, is amplified via phase equilibrium.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanosulfidic photoredox pathway follows the only experimentally demonstrated stepwise route (Patel et al., 2015), but Step 3 (rxn_003), Step 4 (rxn_004), and Step 5 (rxn_005) fail atom and/or mass balance (as validated via deterministic check). The reaction steps otherwise mirror literature, and the inputs/conditions are appropriate for the cited prebiotic scenario. Final hydrolytic steps are routinely assumed but have not been demonstrated for the proline aminonitrile. Hydrolysis is mechanistically plausible but low-yielding. Literature alignment is high, but chemical feasibility is limited by the imbalance and inferred intermediates.
suggestions: Correct stoichiometry and atom balance for reactions rxn_003, rxn_004, and rxn_005; ensure all species (especially S-containing, HCN balance, and any small molecule side products) are explicitly included.
If possible, cite more precise intermediate characterizations and yields from Patel et al. Supplementary Information.
Explicitly annotate any chemically inferred but uncharacterized steps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanamide (arginine) branch is chemically sound up to arginine and ornithine, but the product is not proline (as alignment with literature notes), and rxn_004 remains unbalanced. This branch accurately reflects the main competing sink (cyanamide) and is well-justified, but does not lead to the desired target.
suggestions: Clarify endpoint—this branch should terminate at arginine or ornithine and be clearly marked as a non-proline pathway.
Balance rxn_004 or annotate missing side products.
Consider removing as a 'pathway to proline' or explicitly present as a competitive sink.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrothermal cyclization of ornithine/arginine to proline is hypothetical but consistent with one literature report (Vallentyne 1968). Mechanistic details and plausibility for nonenzymatic settings remain uncertain.
suggestions: Mark both steps as speculative, citing Vallentyne 1968 as the only historical evidence.
Model the branching explicitly—including losses, side products, and hyrolysis yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydrothermal protometabolic (metabolism-first, glutamate/P5C) pathway is speculative. Only the initial step (reductive amination to glutamate) has experimental support. The subsequent steps (Glu→P5C, P5C→Pro) are not demonstrated prebiotically, with the final reduction especially problematic. Marked as speculative in line with literature.
suggestions: Label rxn_014 as not demonstrated and speculative.
Clarify that Glu-to-GSA (carboxylate reduction) has not been achieved under plausible prebiotic conditions.
Remove or segregate these steps if using for only experimentally supported networks.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Spark discharge ('Miller') Strecker synthesis of proline is represented here by a detection-based route; rxn_015 is unbalanced and only inferred (no direct mechanism shown in literature). The presence of proline in Miller-style experiments is robust, but the reaction mechanism is only an educated guess.
suggestions: Explicitly mark this route as having no mechanistic demonstration.
Correct the mass/atom balance for rxn_015.
Present only as a detection-based observation, not as a resolved mechanistic pathway.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Represents interstellar ice photolysis and hydrolysis-dependent detection: accounts for documented observations in the literature but offers no mechanism. Environment and product identity (proline released after acid hydrolysis) fit consensus. Reasonable as a 'detection only' representation.
suggestions: Maintain clear annotation of this route as 'detection only'—hydrolysis from macro-organic residue.
Avoid over-interpretation of environmental detail.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Asteroidal/meteoritic parent body route is a detection-only pathway in line with literature. Proline (including as a free or bound fraction) is observed in Bennu and Murchison. Suitable as an observational branch.
suggestions: Continue to label this as hydrolysis-based and non-mechanistic.
If possible, distinguish free and bound (hydrolyzed) proline products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Nebular Fischer-Tropsch-type (FTT) catalysis is included as a plausible but unproven route. Literature highlights a lack of proline-specific evidence for FTT, so this should be noted as hypothetical and detection only.
suggestions: Annotate as mechanistically unresolved and not proline-specific.
If possible, cite the exact studies and clarify the limitations of detection.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Phase-behavior chiral amplification (eutectic enrichment) aligns precisely with experimental data for proline (Klussmann et al. 2006), including limitations (solvent relevance, seed ee). This step is well supported.
suggestions: Continue to note solvent caveat (CHCl3) for maximal amplification.
Clarify that solid-phase racemate is persistent ('kinetic trap').

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chirality transfer/amplification by circularly polarized light (CPL) or sugars is experimentally demonstrated for proline analogs (with plausible transfer), and is annotated as such. Literature alignment is strong.
suggestions: Continue to mark as mechanistic amplification, not spontaneous L-proline formation.
Reference signal magnitude from photolysis/CPL papers.

evaluation.network_feedback: The synthesis network is comprehensive and well-structured, reflecting current literature: the cyanosulfidic pathway (P1) reproduces the only experimentally supported stepwise route but has major chemical feasibility issues (mass/atom balance failures in rxn_003, rxn_004, rxn_005, rxn_015). Detection-based meteorite/ice/delivery branches (P6, P7) are appropriate and capture the state of evidence. Metabolism-first (P4) and Orn/Arg cyclization (P3) capture speculative pathways faithfully. Chiral amplification steps are modeled in line with consistent experimental evidence. To move the overall network from 'good' to 'excellent', problematic reactions must be explicitly rebalanced or revised—particularly those failing the deterministic check. With these corrections, network validity and chemical feasibility would rise to approval threshold.
